A prawn is a small, water-dwelling creature with a hard shell on the outside of its body. It belongs to a group of animals called crustaceans — the same broad family as crabs and lobsters. Prawns are found all over the world, in oceans, seas, rivers, and lakes.---
What does a prawn look like?

A prawn has a long, narrow body that is slightly curved. Its body is divided into segments, a bit like the sections of a pill capsule joined together. This segmented body is protected by a hard outer shell called an exoskeleton — think of it as a suit of armour that the prawn wears on the outside instead of having bones on the inside.

At the front, it has a pointed, blade-like projection sticking out between its eyes, called a rostrum. It has two long, thin antennae (feelers) that it uses to sense its surroundings. It also has ten legs — five pairs — which it uses for walking along the sea floor, and smaller limb-like structures under its belly called swimmerets, which help it move through the water. At the tail end, it has a fan-shaped fin that it can snap powerfully to propel itself backwards when escaping danger.

Most prawns are translucent (semi-see-through) or grey when alive, but they turn pink or reddish-orange when cooked — this is something most people recognise instantly.

Most prawns live in saltwater — in oceans and seas. However, some species (varieties) live in freshwater, in rivers and lakes. They tend to live near the bottom of the water, on sandy or muddy floors, where they scavenge for food like small plants, algae, and tiny organic matter.

Prawns, like all crustaceans, cannot grow inside a rigid shell. So as they get bigger, they shed their old shell — a process called moulting — and grow a new, larger one. Just after moulting, while the new shell is still soft, a prawn is vulnerable to predators.

Prawns range greatly in size depending on the species. Small ones can be just a few centimetres long. Large ones, like the Giant Tiger Prawn, can grow up to about 30 centimetres (roughly the length of a ruler). In food markets, you'll often see them labelled by size: medium, large, jumbo, etc.
Prawn vs. Shrimp — what's the difference?

This is one of the most important and most misunderstood things about the word "prawn."

In everyday language, the words prawn and shrimp are used almost interchangeably in most parts of the world — they refer to the same type of creature in casual speech. However, whether people say "prawn" or "shrimp" depends largely on where in the world they live:

  • In British English (used in the UK, Australia, India, South Africa, and many other countries), the word "prawn" is the standard, everyday word for these creatures. If you're in India and you order seafood, you'll almost always see it called "prawn" on the menu.
  • In American English, the word "shrimp" is the standard term for the very same creature.

So if a person in Mumbai says "prawn curry," and a person in New York says "shrimp curry," they are almost certainly talking about the same dish.

Scientifically, however, prawns and shrimp are actually two different but closely related types of creatures. The technical differences include the structure of their gills and the way their body segments overlap. Prawns technically belong to a group called Dendrobranchiata and shrimp to Pleocyemata. But these distinctions matter mainly to scientists and marine biologists — in everyday life, the words are used loosely and interchangeably.

Prawns are one of the most widely eaten seafoods in the world. They are prized for their sweet, mild, slightly oceanic flavour and their firm, juicy texture. They can be cooked in countless ways: grilled, fried, steamed, boiled, added to curries, pasta, stir-fries, salads, and soups.

When sold in food markets or restaurants, prawns may come:

  • Shell-on — with the full outer shell still intact (more flavourful when cooked this way)
  • Peeled / shelled — with the shell removed for convenience
  • Deveined — with a thin dark vein (the digestive tract) removed from the back, which is common in larger prawns for aesthetic and taste reasons
  • Raw — grey and uncooked
  • Cooked — already pink and ready to eat

• "She ordered a plate of garlic prawns at the restaurant."
  • "The fisherman brought in a fresh catch of prawns this morning."
  • "Prawn curry is a popular dish along the coastal regions of India."
  • "He peeled the prawns before adding them to the pasta."

A prawn is a small, shelled, ten-legged sea (or freshwater) creature that is eaten as seafood all over the world. It has a segmented body, long antennae, and a fan-shaped tail. It turns pink when cooked. The word "prawn" is the standard British/Indian English term for what Americans call a "shrimp" — the two words point to the same creature in everyday life, even though scientists distinguish between them. Prawns are beloved worldwide for their delicious flavour and are used in a vast range of dishes across many cuisines.
